The hardware includes two Imlac PDS-1 consoles, each with 8K 16-bit words of memory, and a DEC 340 display with a light pen, a Rand Tablet and a Lincoln Wand. It was written for the network graphics meeting in RFC 134.

today: RFC 174 is a historical snapshot of 1970s graphics technology. The Imlac PDS-1 and DEC 340 systems are now museum pieces, but the software concepts like SMOG and MOVIE pioneered interactive graphics programming techniques still relevant to modern graphics systems.

sections.title: UCLA's Graphics Setup
sections.content:
RFC 174 describes the computer graphics hardware and software available in the UCLA Computer Science Department in 1971. The document was submitted for the network graphics meeting mentioned in RFC 134, so other sites could see what equipment UCLA could contribute to collaborative graphics research.

UCLA had two main graphics systems: the Imlac PDS-1 graphics consoles and the DEC 340 Display Station with associated devices.
sections.eli5: UCLA wanted to tell the network what screens and drawing tools they had, so other sites would know what they could work with.

sections.title: Graphics Hardware
sections.content:
The Imlac PDS-1 was the primary graphics console at UCLA. The department had two units, each with 8K 16-bit words of memory. The display screens were mounted with the long axis vertical for optimal graphics work.

The DEC 340 Display Station complemented the Imlac systems. It came equipped with a light pen for interactive pointing, a Rand Tablet for input, and a Lincoln Wand for three-dimensional positioning. A dedicated display processor drove the DEC 340, reading instructions from an XDS Sigma 7 computer memory via a dedicated memory port.
sections.eli5: They had two types of drawing machines: screens with about 8,000 words of memory each, and a more advanced display screen with a pen you could point at pictures with.

sections.title: Software and Applications
sections.content:
The Imlac PDS-1 systems used the Imlac-provided text and graphics support software to function as alphanumeric and graphics consoles at 1200 baud. These systems were used only with the SEX timesharing system at UCLA.

For the DEC 340, UCLA had developed a comprehensive library of routines called SMOG (Sub-program Manager for On-Line Graphics) that interfaced with FORTRAN programs. Using these facilities, UCLA had implemented several graphics applications: MOSAIC, an experimental program for manipulating polar coordinate equations to explore interesting images; FISHEYE, which demonstrated novel image mapping techniques to show large images on small screens; and MOVIE, a scenario language for composing animated sequences, with automatic camera control.
sections.eli5: UCLA had written programs like MOSAIC to draw patterns, FISHEYE to show big pictures on small screens, and MOVIE to make animations. These ran on their special graphics machines.
